title: The Twelve Apostles
lead: The Twelve were the inner group Jesus chose and sent out with his authority, a sign of Israel's twelve tribes renewed. The New Testament also uses "apostle," one sent, for others such as Paul, Barnabas and Junia.

sections.b: Four lists name the Twelve (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). They agree on most names and order them in three groups of four, led by Peter, Philip and James son of Alphaeus. They included fishermen, a tax collector and a "zealot." Matthias replaced Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:15–26).

The number points to Jacob's twelve sons and Israel's tribes. Jesus promises the Twelve thrones "judging the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30), and the New Jerusalem has their names on its foundations (Revelation 21:14). Many historians see the choice of twelve as a sign that Jesus looked for the restoration of all Israel.

Paul calls himself an apostle (Galatians 1:1) and counts others too: James the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19), and probably Andronicus and Junia (Romans 16:7). That last verse is debated: it may mean they were "well known among the apostles" or only "well known to the apostles," and some have read the second name as a man's name, Junias. Acts also calls Barnabas an apostle (Acts 14:14). Churches differ on whether the apostles' authority passes to bishops in succession (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican) or lives on in the apostles' teaching in Scripture (most Protestants).
